title: One-way doors vs. two-way doors
body: Some decisions are one-way doors: hard to reverse, worth deliberating widely. Most are two-way doors: cheap to undo, best made fast by whoever is closest to the problem. Most teams slow down two-way doors as if they were one-way.

title: The tiebreaker
body: Your team is split 50/50 on a technical approach and you're the tiebreaker. What's the better move?

options.label: Decide based on your own past experience alone
Set a deadline, get a one-page tradeoff writeup from each side against shared criteria, then decide
Wait until the team reaches consensus

explanation: Forcing the tradeoffs onto paper against shared criteria makes the decision about the evidence, not about who argues loudest — and it keeps you from waiting indefinitely for consensus that may never come.

title: Three weeks on a two-way door
body: A team spent three weeks debating which analytics tool to adopt — a cheap, reversible choice — while a genuine one-way-door decision, a data model migration, got rushed through in two days. The cost was not the decisions, it was matching the wrong speed to each.

title: Ask how expensive it is to reverse
body: Before your next contentious decision, write one sentence: 'If we're wrong, how expensive is it to undo?' Let the answer set how much time the decision deserves.

title: Separate the decision from the decision-maker
body: A good process run by the wrong person fails. A bad process run by the right person still fails. Make sure whoever owns the call is the person closest to living with its consequences.

title: Write the decision down
body: One paragraph: the decision, the alternatives you considered, and why. It forces clarity in the moment and saves you from re-litigating it three months later.

title: No single owner
body: A cross-functional project has no single owner, and decisions keep stalling while everyone waits for consensus. What is the fix?

options.label: Name a single decision-maker for the project, even if others stay consulted or informed
Put every decision to a team vote
Let whoever raises an issue loudest decide it

explanation: Shared ownership across a group is usually no ownership at all. A single named decision-maker, with others clearly consulted or informed, is what actually unblocks stalled cross-functional calls.

title: Pre-mortem before you commit
body: Before locking in a big call, spend ten minutes imagining it failed and writing down why. It surfaces risks that confidence quietly hides.

title: Set the decision deadline before the debate
body: Open-ended discussions expand to fill whatever time is available. A deadline, set in advance, forces the group toward a call instead of circling it.

title: The decision that kept re-opening
body: Every time someone new joined the team, they asked "wait, why did we choose this?" — and the debate restarted from zero, because nobody had written the reasoning down. A two-paragraph decision log would have saved months.

title: Beware the decision that feels unanimous
body: If everyone agrees instantly, someone probably has not voiced a concern yet. Ask directly, "what would make this wrong?" before moving on.

title: Put a date on a stuck decision
body: Find one decision currently stuck in "more discussion needed." Set a decision date for it this week, even if the analysis isn't complete.

title: Six months invested, new information
body: You've spent six months building an approach, and new information suggests it's wrong. The team feels invested. What actually matters here?

options.label: Finish it — you have already invested the time
Evaluate the path forward fresh, as if starting today, ignoring what's already spent
Compromise by building half of the original plan
Figure out who originally chose this approach

explanation: The time already spent is gone either way — it cannot be recovered by finishing. The only thing that should drive the decision is which path is best starting from right now.

title: Reversible calls deserve a bias toward action
body: Waiting for perfect information on a two-way door often costs more than just trying the cheaper option and adjusting once you learn something.
